messages.content: I am cleaning an old camping lantern at my kitchen table. The glass is cloudy and I keep leaving fingerprints on it.
I have been there. What is inside the lantern?
It belonged to my aunt Belen. She used to take it fishing, although she rarely caught anything. I like that it has been useful to somebody.
That gives it a little history. Is the cloudy glass something that can be fixed, or are you going to keep using it for a while?
I have taken the glass out now. There is a dead moth inside. That must have been an ambitious last evening.
Was it a good catch, or the end of a good evening?
I am making tea while it dries. Do you keep old things because you like them, or only because they still work?
I dislike the dead moth. The lantern would be a different story if it could tell you whether I was being sentimental.
The moth has been given a burial in the compost. The lantern is keeping its place on my shelf. I am sentimental about it, whether that is sensible or not.
You are not alone in that. Some things have a place in our lives even when we don't love them much.
Belen once dropped it into a puddle and blamed the weather. That is the family approach to admitting mistakes.
Her lantern tells a different story. It did not leave the house on its own account.
I am keeping the little dent in the base. If I polished away everything that happened to it, I would hardly recognise it.
I like that. I can imagine an evening with a glass lantern you know, rather than an evening with a story you have written.
The glass is clean now. I am going to make a sandwich before I find something else to take apart.
Go ahead. The lantern can wait another minute.
Who was responsible for your instruction when you joined the community?
Mara was my teacher. She could make an ordinary mistake difficult to hide from.
Are you able to visit that person these days?
No. She died some years ago. I remember her, but remembering does not give me another chance to ask a question.
